summary: This memo describes the US top-level domains on the Internet, replacing RFC 1386. It explains how names under .us are organised by geography.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1480 describes how the United States organized computer names ending in .US. It sets out geographic name branches and explains how organizations could register names or manage a delegated part of the domain.

subtitle: The 1993 plan for organizing names under the United States top-level domain.

tldr.problem: The US Domain needed a manageable structure for registering computers, schools, agencies, and other organizations under .US.
tldr.mechanism: Names follow a hierarchy based mainly on state and locality, with separate branches for groups such as schools, libraries, and government agencies. A branch can be entered directly or delegated to a manager operating name servers.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1480 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1386. It describes the US Domain's naming and administration rules as of June 1993.

today: RFC 1480 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 1386. It records the US Domain's rules as of June 1993, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Purpose of the US Domain
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) stores names and information in a distributed database. RFC 1480 describes the US Domain, an official top-level domain using the country code US. The memo says any computer in the United States may be registered there.

At the time, many US organizations used EDU or COM instead. The US Domain was intended to provide a structured place for computers associated with schools, government, libraries, businesses, and other groups.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS organizes computer names so people can use names instead of numeric addresses. The .US branch is the part of that system described in this memo.

sections.title: Names Follow Geographic and Organizational Branches
sections.content:
The basic hierarchy places a state code below US, then a locality such as a city or county, and then an organization or computer. State codes use the two-letter US postal abbreviations. For example, a locality name may appear as BERKELEY.CA.US.

The memo also defines special branches. FED is for federal agencies, DNI for distributed national institutes, and branches such as K12, CC, TEC, LIB, STATE, and GEN cover schools and other groups within states. The added levels help distinguish names and divide administration.
sections.plainLanguage: A name shows its place in the hierarchy, such as state and locality. Special branches identify groups that need their own part of the naming system.

sections.title: Direct Registration and Delegation
sections.content:
A registration can be entered directly in the main database or handled through delegation. With delegation, an organization manages a branch and runs its name servers. Applicants provide administrator and technical contacts through the US Domain registration process.

A delegated zone must have at least two independent name servers in physically separate locations. Its manager must treat applicants equally, process requests in a timely way, and tell the higher-level administrator about changes to servers or contact details. The memo says a host registration usually took a few days, followed by a name-server update 12 to 24 hours later.
sections.plainLanguage: A person or organization could register a name with the central administrator or ask to manage a branch. A branch manager needed two separate name servers and had to follow the same rules for every applicant.

sections.title: Zones, Records, and Wildcards
sections.content:
DNS data is divided into zones. A zone's authoritative name servers hold the official data, and each zone must be available from at least two servers. Records describe names and information such as addresses, aliases, and mail forwarders.

A wildcard record can apply to names below a domain, but not to the domain itself. RFC 1480 allows wildcards under some organizational branches but not under city or state domains. The authors prefer explicit records because wildcards can hide which individual hosts exist.
sections.plainLanguage: A zone is a managed part of DNS data, and at least two servers must be able to answer for it. A wildcard can cover many names, but it can also make individual hosts harder to see.
